title: Cost pressure and public-service concern remain dominant while AI optimism fragments around convenience, trust, and risk
source_unit: Office for National Statistics, Public opinions and social trends, Great Britain: June 2026
geography: Great Britain adults, Opinions and Lifestyle Survey data collected 3-28 June 2026

denominator.unit: Great Britain adult issue-selection question frame

cost_of_living_issue.unit: percent reporting cost of living as an important issue facing the UK

nhs_issue.unit: percent reporting the NHS as an important issue

economy_issue.unit: percent reporting the economy as an important issue

other_pressure_surface.value: crime 61%, immigration 59%, employment 54%, climate and environment 53%, and housing 52%

observations.method: ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey multiple-response question on issues facing the UK; respondents could select more than one option.
observations.uncertainty: The issue shares are perceptions at one field period, are not mutually exclusive, and do not measure objective exposure, policy causation, or priority ranking beyond the question wording.
observations.subgroup: Adults in Great Britain, with age and other subgroup comparisons where published.
observations.counterinterpretation: High issue salience can reflect attention, media coverage, or political interpretation as well as direct household experience; multiple concerns can coexist without a single common cause.

observations.period: 3-28 June 2026; perceived personal benefit from AI

denominator.unit: Great Britain adult AI-benefit question frame

ai_benefit_agree.unit: percent agreeing or strongly agreeing that AI will benefit them

ai_benefit_disagree.unit: percent disagreeing or strongly disagreeing that AI will benefit them

younger_adult_benefit.value: 47% among ages 16-29 and 45% among ages 30-49 agreed or strongly agreed

observations.method: ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey question on whether artificial intelligence will benefit respondents; estimates are compared with earlier ONS waves.
observations.uncertainty: The question captures perceived personal benefit, not actual adoption, productivity, job quality, consumer outcomes, or long-run welfare; the AI definition has changed slightly over time.
observations.subgroup: Great Britain adults, especially age groups 16-29, 30-49, and older adults.
observations.counterinterpretation: Uncertainty or neutrality may represent lack of information rather than opposition; perceived benefit can coexist with concern about institutions, work, data, or news.

observations.period: 3-28 June 2026; perceived positive uses of AI

denominator.unit: Great Britain adult AI-positive-impact question frame

learning_access.unit: percent reporting improved access to learning or education as a possible positive impact

job_easier.unit: percent reporting making their job easier as a possible positive impact

household_tasks_easier.unit: percent reporting making household tasks easier as a possible positive impact

no_positive_impact.unit: percent saying AI could not have a positive impact on their lives

observations.method: ONS multiple-response question on possible positive impacts of AI in respondents' lives.
observations.uncertainty: These are anticipated uses rather than observed behavior or delivered benefits; categories can overlap and do not measure access, quality, time saved, or distribution of gains.
observations.subgroup: Great Britain adults considering AI effects on education, paid work, and household tasks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low reported benefit may reflect unfamiliarity or limited access; convenience gains can also increase expectations, surveillance, workload, or dependence on platforms.

observations.period: 3-28 June 2026; perceived AI risks and information trust

denominator.unit: Great Britain adult AI-risk question frame

more_risks_than_benefits.unit: percent saying AI brings more risks than benefits

more_benefits_than_risks.unit: percent saying AI brings more benefits than risks

fake_information_risk.unit: percent reporting difficulty telling whether news or information is fake as a negative AI impact

personal_data_risk.unit: percent reporting use of personal data without consent as a negative AI impact

cybercrime_risk.unit: percent reporting increased chances of experiencing cybercrime as a negative AI impact

observations.method: ONS questions on relative AI risks and benefits and possible negative impacts, using the June 2026 Opinions and Lifestyle Survey frame.
observations.uncertainty: Risk perceptions are not incident rates or verified harms; the measures do not identify which systems cause concern, whether concerns change behavior, or whether safeguards reduce perceived risk.
observations.subgroup: Great Britain adults concerned about information authenticity, data consent, cybercrime, and AI governance.
observations.counterinterpretation: High concern can indicate demand for trustworthy design and regulation rather than rejection of AI; perceived risk may rise as public awareness improves.

related_sources.claim: WEF Global Risks Report 2026 provides complementary global evidence on misinformation, AI trust, and societal polarization.
OECD Going Digital Measurement Roadmap 2026 provides complementary measurement and wellbeing context for digital transformation.

boundary: This record adds an official public-sentiment route connecting cost-of-living and public-service salience with AI expectations, household convenience, information authenticity, privacy, and cyber-risk. It retains ONS findings as aggregate perception measures, not respondent-level predictions, objective incident rates, causal technology effects, or proof that perceived benefits or risks determine adoption and political action.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ONS June 2026 bulletin was retrieved and reviewed for issue salience, AI-benefit expectations, positive-use categories, risk-benefit balance, and negative-impact perceptions.
